title: A Survey on Swarming With Micro Air Vehicles: Fundamental Challenges and Constraints

subsections.content:
Swarm coordination and collective behavior in micro air vehicle (MAV) systems are fundamentally inspired by biological swarms, where global order emerges from local interactions among simple agents. Drawing from swarm intelligence principles, decentralized control architectures rely on stigmergy and self-organization to achieve coherent motion without centralized command, as demonstrated in social insect colonies ref [19]. Engineering implementations often employ attraction-repulsion force fields to maintain swarm cohesion and spacing, with stable aggregations achieved through carefully designed odd-function potentials that balance proximity and collision avoidance ref [2]. Recent advances in aerial swarms have integrated evolutionary optimization to tune flocking parameters for real-world constraints such as communication delays and confined spaces, enabling stable collective motion in large flocks of up to 30 drones ref [3].

Notably, some bioinspired approaches eschew traditional collision avoidance altogether, instead designing robots to withstand and recover from collisions—mirroring the low-penalty dynamics observed in natural swarms like bees and bats ref [5]. This resilience enables simpler motion planners and reduces computational overhead, making it particularly suitable for resource-constrained MAVs. The broader swarm engineering perspective emphasizes systematic design methodologies that link individual rules to emergent behaviors, advocating for rigorous validation through both simulation and hardware experiments ref [20]. Together, these approaches highlight a paradigm shift from deterministic trajectory planning to emergent, adaptive coordination grounded in biological principles and robust to environmental uncertainty.

Swarm architecture and system design for micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) emphasize modularity, decentralization, and scalability to enable robust collective behavior. The Distributed Flight Array (DFA) exemplifies a distributed architecture where simple, single-propeller modules autonomously dock and form stable flying configurations, demonstrating how minimal individual intelligence can yield complex collective dynamics ref [10]. Similarly, ModQuad introduces a cuboid-based modular platform capable of midair self-assembly, using mechanical docking mechanisms to form cooperative flying structures, thereby redefining the notion of a swarm as reconfigurable physical entities ref [11]. Complementing this, the Design and Control of Aerial Modules for Inflight Self-Disassembly extends the concept by enabling controlled fragmentation during flight, allowing dynamic adaptation to task or environmental changes ref [12]. The Flying Gripper further illustrates functional specialization through modular aggregation, where four quadrotor modules form a four-bar linkage to grasp and transport objects, showcasing how physical coupling enables new capabilities beyond individual agent functions ref [13]. In contrast, VIO-Swarm presents a vision-based architecture that eliminates external localization infrastructure by leveraging onboard visual-inertial odometry, enabling scalable, GPS-denied operation with up to 12 quadrotors ref [8]. The SFly project integrates these principles with a full-stack approach, combining custom hexacopter hardware, real-time monocular SLAM, and distributed optimization for surveillance missions, highlighting the necessity of co-designing perception, control, and communication layers ref [7]. The Crazyflie 2.0 platform, while smaller in scale, provides an accessible, open-source foundation for rapid prototyping of swarm algorithms, lowering the barrier to entry for distributed system experimentation ref [10].

Collective system design must balance computational load, communication overhead, and physical constraints. Modular architectures like those in ModQuad and DFA reduce per-unit complexity by distributing computation and control, while enabling fault tolerance through redundancy. The integration of passive mechanical docking systems—such as those in ModQuad and the Flying Gripper—minimizes energy expenditure during reconfiguration, a critical consideration for battery-constrained MAVs. Meanwhile, vision-based localization in VIO-Swarm and SFly eliminates reliance on external infrastructure, enhancing deployment flexibility in GPS-denied or indoor environments. These systems collectively underscore a paradigm shift from monolithic, centrally controlled swarms toward heterogeneous, self-organizing architectures that fuse physical reconfigurability with distributed autonomy.

subsections.subsection_title: Hardware and Embedded Systems for MAV Swarms
subsections.content:
The hardware and embedded systems underpinning MAV swarms demand extreme miniaturization, low power consumption, and high computational efficiency to enable autonomous collective behavior. Recent advances have yielded ultra-lightweight autopilots such as the Lisa-S, weighing just 2.8 grams and integrating an IMU, magnetometer, GPS, and a 32-bit processor—all on a 2×2 cm board—enabling GPS-based autonomous missions on sub-30 g platforms ref [15]. Similarly, the design of pico quadrotors with 25 g mass incorporates robust mechanical cages and compact embedded systems to withstand collisions while maintaining flight stability ref [16]. For GPS-denied environments, vision-based systems have emerged as critical alternatives; the Edge-FS algorithm, running on a 4 g stereo camera with an STM32F4 microprocessor, enables velocity estimation and obstacle avoidance using edge-based optical flow and stereo disparity at 20 Hz ref [8]. Lightweight omnidirectional vision sensors, as light as 2.6 g, facilitate bioinspired navigation by computing wide-field optic flow onboard 30 g MAVs for corridor navigation without external positioning ref [18]. Low-cost time-of-flight sensors like the VL53L0X provide reliable proximity detection under varying lighting and surface conditions, offering an energy-efficient solution for collision avoidance in cluttered spaces ref [20]. Additionally, optiPilot systems leveraging simple light sensors and minimal computation enable low-altitude autonomous flight by combining optic-flow feedback with basic control laws ref [15]. These systems collectively demonstrate a trend toward sensor-fusion architectures that prioritize computational efficiency and physical resilience over raw processing power.

Navigation systems such as Honeywell’s MEMS-based solution, integrating HG1930 IMU, GPS, barometer, and magnetometer with ECTOS IIc software, illustrate early but foundational efforts in modular, customizable MAV navigation ref [14]. The convergence of these technologies—miniaturized sensors, low-power processors, and efficient algorithms—has enabled the transition from single-MEV autonomy to scalable, robust swarms capable of operating in constrained, GPS-denied environments with minimal infrastructure.

subsections.subsection_title: Perception and Navigation in GPS-Denied Environments
subsections.content:
Autonomous navigation in GPS-denied environments remains a critical challenge for MAV swarms, particularly in indoor, urban, or cluttered settings where satellite signals are unreliable or absent. Vision-based approaches have emerged as a dominant solution, with systems leveraging monocular cameras and inertial measurement units (IMUs) to achieve real-time state estimation and mapping. Ref. [1] presents the SFLY project, demonstrating fully autonomous navigation using only onboard vision and IMU, enabling 3D mapping and surveillance without external infrastructure. Complementary to this, ref. [4] introduces a closed-form solution for simultaneous attitude and speed estimation from monocular vision and IMU data, eliminating scale drift and initialization dependencies. For computationally constrained platforms, ref. [9] proposes high-frequency state estimation using optical flow sensors and low-cost IMUs, achieving 100 Hz updates with minimal processing overhead. Ref. [10] advances this further with Navion, a dedicated ASIC accelerator for energy-efficient visual-inertial odometry on nano-drones, enabling real-time localization with sub-25 mW power consumption.

To enhance robustness in complex indoor environments, sensor fusion strategies have been widely adopted. Ref. [7] combines monocular visual SLAM with 2D LIDAR and IMU data within an EKF framework, improving pose estimation in ruined buildings. Similarly, ref. [8] integrates 3D LIDAR point clouds with inertial data using a customized ICP algorithm and PCA-based line extraction, enabling efficient localization in obstacle-dense spaces. Ref. [18] further extends this by fusing stereo vision with 2D LIDAR, using laser depth to resolve monocular scale ambiguity and optimize trajectory via ICP registration. For multi-floor navigation, ref. [5] demonstrates loop-closure-aware mapping and autonomous control on a mobile processor, enabling full autonomy without external aids. These approaches collectively underscore the shift from single-sensor reliance to multi-modal, embedded-friendly fusion architectures tailored for swarm-scale deployment.

subsections.subsection_title: Collision Resilience and Safe Operation in Cluttered Environments
subsections.content:
Safe operation of MAV swarms in cluttered environments demands robust collision resilience, extending beyond mere avoidance to include physical robustness and recovery mechanisms. Reactive obstacle avoidance systems leveraging on-board stereo vision have demonstrated low-latency performance, enabling real-time maneuvering without reliance on external computation or high-power CPUs, as shown in systems running at 60 FPS on FPGA platforms ref [29]. Other approaches integrate dynamic path planning with real-time 3D mapping from stereo imagery, allowing autonomous navigation in unknown, dynamic settings ref [34]. An alternative paradigm exploits disparity space for efficient collision checking, projecting trajectories into image space to reduce computational load while maintaining safety guarantees ref [35]. For low-cost platforms, monocular vision-based distance estimation enables frontal obstacle detection in GPS-denied environments with sub-3% error, making it viable for resource-constrained swarms ref [11].

Beyond perception-driven avoidance, bio-inspired mechanical resilience offers a complementary strategy: the AirBurr robot, for instance, is designed to exploit collisions rather than avoid them, mimicking insect behavior to recover autonomously after impacts ref [12]. Similarly, insect-inspired dual-stiffness frames absorb kinetic energy during collisions, protecting sensitive components while enabling continued flight—validated on 50g quadrotors subjected to high-speed impacts ref [36]. These mechanical solutions are particularly valuable in environments where sensor failure or latency renders avoidance unreliable. Recent theoretical work quantifies the critical interplay between perception latency, sensor range, and actuation limits, establishing that even minor delays can cap safe flight speeds in dense clutter ref [14]. In industrial confined spaces, where magnetic interference and poor lighting prevail, laser-based localization combined with collision-aware navigation has enabled reliable inspection missions, underscoring the need for sensor fusion and environment-adaptive safety layers ref [20].

subsections.section_title: Intra-Swarm Sensing, Communication, and Collision Avoidance
subsections.content:
Decentralized SLAM and cooperative mapping enable micro air vehicle (MAV) swarms to construct consistent environmental representations without centralized coordination, critical for operations in GPS-denied or dynamic environments. The DDF-SAM 2.0 framework addresses information double-counting in distributed mapping by introducing anti-factors to subtract redundant data from shared neighborhood summaries, enabling consistent augmented local maps while maintaining computational tractability ref [37]. This approach improves upon earlier decentralized SLAM methods by unifying local and peer information within a single graphical model, avoiding overly conservative constraints that degrade map accuracy. Complementary techniques such as distributed graph optimization and consensus-based belief propagation have been adapted for resource-constrained MAVs, allowing scalable mapping with limited bandwidth ref [2]. Recent work has integrated lightweight visual-inertial odometry with decentralized factor graphs to reduce drift and enhance map fidelity in tight spaces ref [3]. Additionally, landmark-based consensus protocols enable swarms to agree on shared feature identities across distributed nodes, mitigating data association ambiguities ref [4]. These methods collectively support robust, real-time cooperative mapping even under intermittent communication and heterogeneous sensor suites.

To ensure scalability, approximation techniques such as sparse information matrices and submap summarization have been proposed to reduce communication overhead without sacrificing global consistency ref [5]. Experimental validation on small MAV platforms demonstrates that decentralized SLAM can achieve map accuracy comparable to centralized systems while preserving autonomy and fault tolerance ref [6]. Emerging hybrid approaches combine range-based sensing with visual features to improve loop closure detection in low-texture environments, further enhancing cooperative mapping reliability ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Intra-Swarm Sensing, Communication, and Collision Avoidance
subsections.subsection_title: Ultra-Wideband and Wireless Communication for Relative Localization
subsections.content:
Ultra-Wideband (UWB) communication has emerged as a robust enabler for relative localization in GPS-denied environments, offering centimeter-level accuracy and high temporal resolution critical for micro air vehicle (MAV) swarms. Ref. [1] demonstrates a cooperative relative localization framework where UAVs exchange inter-vehicle distance measurements via UWB and fuse them with self-displacement data using an extended Kalman filter, achieving stable relative positioning even under dynamic motion. This approach is particularly effective in scenarios where static beacons are deployed to initialize local coordinate frames, as shown in flight experiments with multiple quadcopters. In contrast, Ref. [2] presents a one-way UWB system where robots passively receive signals from fixed anchors, enabling scalable, low-latency self-localization suitable for high-speed control loops—ideal for MAVs operating in confined spaces without requiring peer-to-peer communication.

Beyond UWB, other wireless protocols have been explored for relative localization with lower hardware overhead. Ref. [3] leverages Bluetooth signal strength (RSSI) to estimate inter-MAV ranges, fusing this with exchanged state estimates (velocity, orientation) to enable collision avoidance in tight indoor environments with minimal computational load. While less accurate than UWB, such methods offer cost and power advantages for lightweight platforms. A comparative analysis in Ref. [4] highlights UWB’s superior range resolution and interference resilience over Bluetooth, ZigBee, and Wi-Fi, making it the preferred choice for precision relative localization despite higher complexity. Together, these works illustrate a spectrum of trade-offs between accuracy, scalability, and resource constraints in wireless-based relative localization for MAV swarms.

subsections.section_title: Intra-Swarm Sensing, Communication, and Collision Avoidance
subsections.content:
Audio-based localization and sensing offer a lightweight, communication-free alternative for relative positioning in micro air vehicle (MAV) swarms, particularly in GPS-denied or visually cluttered environments. By leveraging onboard microphone arrays, MAVs can detect and localize sound sources emitted by teammates or environmental beacons, enabling relative bearing estimation without external infrastructure. The ManyEars open framework provides a modular, real-time solution for sound source localization and separation using multi-microphone arrays, adaptable to robotic platforms through open hardware and ROS integration ref [42]. Building on this, Basiri et al. demonstrated a cooperative audio-based localization method where MAVs estimate their position by perceiving a sound-emitting beacon, fusing bearing measurements with inertial data to achieve robust self-localization without communication networks ref [43]. Subsequent work extended this to 3-D relative direction estimation between drones using engine noise and active acoustic signaling, enabling identity discrimination and extended detection range even in noisy flight conditions ref [44]. To support algorithm development, the AIRA-UAS corpus was introduced as the first dataset of onboard UAV audio recordings, capturing ego-noise and inter-drone acoustic signals during dynamic maneuvers, facilitating benchmarking of localization and separation algorithms in realistic scenarios ref [45].

These approaches overcome payload and power constraints inherent to small MAVs, avoiding reliance on bulky sensors or external positioning systems. Active acoustic signaling improves reliability in high-noise environments, while coherence-based signal processing enables robust bearing estimation despite Doppler shifts and multipath effects. The integration of audio sensing with inertial navigation allows for continuous state estimation, making it suitable for formation control and collision avoidance in dense swarms. Future directions include multi-source separation in dynamic environments, energy-efficient acoustic transceivers, and hybrid systems combining audio with inertial or optical cues to enhance accuracy under varying flight conditions.

subsections.section_title: Intra-Swarm Sensing, Communication, and Collision Avoidance
subsections.content:
Collision avoidance and reactive navigation in micro air vehicle (MAV) swarms demand decentralized, real-time decision-making under limited sensing and computational resources. A foundational approach is the use of velocity obstacles (VO), which define forbidden velocity regions that would lead to collisions with moving or static obstacles; this framework has been extended to reciprocal velocity obstacles (RVO) to account for mutual reactivity among agents, ensuring oscillation-free navigation without explicit communication ref [52]. The hybrid reciprocal velocity obstacle (HRVO) further refines this by incorporating robot kinematics and sensor uncertainty, enabling robust performance in dense, dynamic environments ref [51]. Recent work has demonstrated the efficacy of RVO variants in commodity quadcopters using ultrasound-based localization, where risk contours adapt dynamically to relative speed and localization confidence, enabling safe operation in GNSS-denied indoor spaces ref [46]. Bioinspired models, derived from human pedestrian behavior, offer human-friendly navigation patterns that emerge naturally in swarms, reducing perceived aggression and improving coexistence in shared spaces ref [48]. Comparative studies between RVO, HRVO, and human-inspired heuristics reveal trade-offs in trajectory efficiency, safety, and emergent collective behaviors under realistic sensing conditions ref [47]. These reactive methods are particularly suited for MAVs due to their low computational overhead and independence from centralized coordination, making them ideal for large-scale swarms where communication bandwidth is constrained ref [50].

In aerial contexts, the three-dimensional nature of flight introduces additional complexity, requiring 3D extensions of velocity-based methods that account for vertical dynamics and acceleration limits ref [13]. While traditional VO approaches assume constant velocity predictions, modern adaptations integrate probabilistic motion models to handle uncertainty in sensor data and actuator delays ref [9]. Experimental validation on real MAV platforms, such as the iRobot Create and custom quadcopters, confirms that reciprocal methods achieve collision-free navigation even in high-density scenarios with hundreds of agents ref [52]. Simulation-based fault injection has further proven critical in tuning parameters for robustness against sensor drift and communication loss, as demonstrated in ultrasound-based systems ref [46]. The convergence of bioinspired heuristics with geometric collision avoidance suggests a promising direction for next-generation swarm navigation systems that balance safety, efficiency, and social acceptability.

subsections.section_title: Intra-Swarm Sensing, Communication, and Collision Avoidance
subsections.subsection_title: Vision-Based Relative Localization and Formation Control
subsections.content:
Vision-based relative localization and formation control in micro air vehicle (MAV) swarms has emerged as a key enabler for fully decentralized operations without reliance on external positioning systems. Recent work by Montijano et al. ref [55] presents a distributed 3-D control law that concurrently regulates relative orientations and positions using onboard cameras and IMU data, achieving stable formation through structure-from-motion pose estimation. Complementing this, Schiano et al. ref [15] introduce a rigidity-based bearing formation controller that operates without reciprocal measurements or a common reference frame, leveraging bearing-only visual feedback to stabilize directed 3-D formations. For markerless operation, Schilling et al. ref [59] demonstrate that convolutional neural networks can learn flocking behaviors directly from raw omnidirectional images, enabling collision avoidance and cohesion without communication or visual tags. Similarly, Faigl et al. ref [13] propose a low-cost embedded system using circular pattern detection to achieve real-time relative localization at 60 Hz, suitable for feedback-based swarm stabilization. Cognetti et al. ref [11] extend mutual localization to anonymous bearing measurements, allowing pose estimation without agent identification—critical for scalable swarms. Reciprocal collision avoidance using visual detection has also been validated by Roelofsen et al. ref [58], who employ fish-eye cameras and probabilistic filtering to track nearby agents and execute safe maneuvers.

Inspired by biological schooling, the principles of local interaction and emergent cohesion—first modeled by Aoki ref [17]—have informed the design of vision-based swarm controllers that prioritize simplicity and robustness. These approaches collectively reduce dependency on communication infrastructure and external infrastructure, aligning with the goals of lightweight, scalable, and resilient aerial swarms. The integration of visual perception with reactive control laws enables MAVs to maintain formation, avoid collisions, and adapt to dynamic environments using only onboard sensing, marking a significant step toward fully autonomous, vision-driven swarm intelligence.

subsections.subsection_title: Simulation and Software Frameworks for Swarm Development
subsections.content:
The development of swarm systems for Micro Air Vehicles (MAVs) relies heavily on simulation frameworks that enable safe, scalable, and repeatable testing of decentralized algorithms. Gazebo, coupled with the Robot Operating System (ROS), has emerged as a foundational platform for high-fidelity quadrotor simulation, offering realistic dynamics, sensor modeling, and environment rendering, as demonstrated in comprehensive frameworks for UAV control and SLAM validation ref [63]. Its integration with ROS has made it a de facto standard for prototyping aerial swarms, though its computational overhead limits scalability for large swarms. To address this, ARGoS was designed as a modular, parallel, multi-engine simulator capable of efficiently simulating tens of thousands of robots through spatial partitioning and multi-threading, achieving near real-time performance even in complex 2D swarm scenarios ref [65]. For aerial-specific applications, AEROSTACK provides a layered software architecture integrating reactive, deliberative, and social robotics layers, enabling fully autonomous multi-UAS missions across five validated aerial platforms ref [66]. AirSim, built on Unreal Engine, delivers photorealistic visual simulation and high-frequency physics for hardware-in-the-loop testing, critical for training vision-based swarm algorithms under diverse environmental conditions ref [67]. Additionally, Buzz introduces a domain-specific programming language for heterogeneous swarms, enabling compositional behavior specification that abstracts low-level communication and supports decentralized execution ref [15]. The vision-based swarm architecture used in the IMAV2013 competition further illustrates the viability of lightweight, marker-assisted localization for indoor swarm coordination without external infrastructure ref [14].

While Gazebo and ARGoS remain dominant for dynamics and scalability respectively, emerging frameworks like AirSim and Buzz are expanding the boundaries of realism and programmability. The modular design of ARGoS allows seamless integration of custom physics engines, while Buzz’s runtime can be layered atop ROS, bridging high-level abstraction with existing toolchains. AEROSTACK’s flight-proven components reduce development time for mission-critical applications, and AirSim’s extensibility supports rapid adaptation to new vehicle types and sensor modalities. Together, these frameworks form a complementary ecosystem that addresses the core challenges of fidelity, scalability, and programmability in swarm development.

subsections.subsection_title: Energy Constraints and Persistent Flight Solutions
subsections.content:
The persistent operation of micro air vehicle (MAV) swarms is fundamentally constrained by the limited energy density of conventional lithium-based batteries, which typically restrict flight durations to 10–20 minutes. To extend mission endurance, researchers have explored alternative energy solutions, including solar power and wireless charging. Ref. [1] demonstrates the first fully solar-powered quadcopter capable of controlled flight beyond the ground effect, achieving 98 seconds of flight under 882 W/m² irradiance without onboard storage—proving the feasibility of solar-only propulsion for small rotorcraft. However, the fragility of unpackaged solar cells and low power-to-weight ratios remain significant hurdles. Alternative approaches leverage autonomous recharging infrastructure. Ref. [3] introduces a wireless power transfer (WPT) system enabling UAVs to recharge without precise landing alignment, reducing control complexity and increasing operational robustness. Similarly, Ref. [7] presents an automatic wireless charging station tolerant of imprecise landings, facilitating continuous operation in unstructured environments.

For missions requiring uninterrupted surveillance, battery swapping offers a more rapid energy replenishment strategy. Ref. [4] and Ref. [5] both describe autonomous 'hot-swap' systems that maintain power continuity during battery replacement, eliminating data loss and minimizing downtime. Ref. [5] further scales this concept with a dual-drum station holding eight batteries, enabling persistent multi-agent missions. Ref. [6] integrates vision-based precision landing with automated recharging to achieve 11 hours of fully autonomous operation, demonstrating the viability of closed-loop energy replenishment for long-term environmental monitoring. Beyond recharge and swap, Ref. [8] explores hydrogen fuel cells as a high-energy-density alternative, designing a VTOL UAV optimized for carrying pressurized hydrogen tanks—offering potential for day-long missions. Collectively, these innovations signal a shift from passive energy constraints to active, infrastructure-enabled persistence in swarm operations.

Human-swarm interaction (HSI) and supervisory control represent critical frontiers in the operational autonomy of micro air vehicle swarms, where the human role transitions from direct pilot to mission supervisor. Recent work emphasizes intuitive, low-cognitive-load interfaces that enhance situation awareness and reduce operator fatigue. A meta-analysis of 27 studies reveals that customizable interfaces and increased swarm autonomy significantly improve performance and reduce cognitive workload, underscoring the need for adaptive human-system designs ref [75]. Spatial gesture recognition, enabled by machine vision and wearable sensors, allows natural selection and command of swarm agents without physical controllers, offering a deviceless interaction paradigm ref [76]. Complementing this, tactile feedback systems like SwarmTouch leverage impedance-controlled formations and vibrotactile patterns to convey swarm dynamics directly through hand contact, improving user immersion and control precision ref [77]. Virtual reality interfaces further extend immersion, enabling operators to visualize and modify complex missions—such as 3D spray painting—in a spatially intuitive environment ref [79]. An ecological interface design approach, grounded in perceptual cues and task-specific affordances, has been shown to support high-level mission management for swarms of four or more UAVs, moving beyond single-UAV telemetry displays ref [9]. Emerging paradigms also leverage commercially available platforms like tablets and smartphones to lower entry barriers and enable real-time, low-latency control ref [80].

Despite these advances, challenges persist in scaling HSI to large swarms, maintaining situational awareness under dynamic conditions, and standardizing evaluation metrics. Current systems often require per-agent adjustments, limiting scalability beyond small teams ref [9]. Future directions include multimodal interfaces combining gesture, voice, haptics, and augmented reality, alongside AI-driven predictive assistance to anticipate operator intent. Standardized benchmarks for HSI efficacy, informed by cognitive load and mission success metrics, remain underdeveloped but are essential for progress in this rapidly evolving domain.

subsections.subsection_title: Autonomous Swarm Coordination for Persistent Operations
subsections.content: Autonomous swarm coordination for persistent operations demands robust, scalable, and decentralized control architectures capable of sustaining mission objectives over indefinite durations. Recent advances have integrated formal methods with swarm robotics to encode persistent surveillance tasks as temporal logic specifications, enabling automatic generation of collision-free, resource-aware trajectories that account for replenishment constraints and time-windowed service requirements. Ref [2] introduces the Persistent Vehicle Routing Problem (P-VRP) and Time-Window Temporal Logic (TWTL), providing a rigorous framework for synthesizing infinite-horizon missions with battery constraints and refueling stations. To ensure operational resilience, decentralized fault detection mechanisms are critical; Ref [7] proposes a generic, scalable, and decentralized approach for identifying faulty agents through local behavioral anomalies, while Ref [8] validates this strategy on physical robot swarms across multiple tasks, demonstrating high detection accuracy under dynamic conditions. These fault-tolerant mechanisms are essential for maintaining swarm integrity during prolonged missions. Furthermore, Ref [13] presents a unified communication protocol based on MAVLink to enable decentralized management and maintenance coordination among MAV swarms, facilitating dynamic task reassignment and health-aware routing. Integrating these components—formal mission specification, decentralized fault diagnosis, and standardized communication—creates a cohesive foundation for persistent, autonomous swarm operations in complex, real-world environments.

subsections.section_title: The Challenge of Local Sensing and Control
subsections.subsection_title: Onboard Sensing and Navigation for Autonomous Swarms
subsections.content:
Onboard sensing and navigation for autonomous micro aerial vehicle (MAV) swarms demand lightweight, energy-efficient systems capable of simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) under strict Size, Weight, and Power (SWAP) constraints. Recent advances in visual-inertial odometry have enabled quadrotors as light as 250g to autonomously navigate cluttered indoor environments using only a stereo camera and IMU, concurrently generating semi-dense 3D maps without external infrastructure ref [85]. These systems leverage complementary sensor fusion to mitigate drift and latency, critical for real-time swarm coordination in GPS-denied settings. The scalability of such approaches is further demonstrated in agile 75g micro quadrotors, where onboard attitude estimation and control enable dense, coordinated flight formations essential for swarm operations ref [3]. To maintain autonomy at scale, computational efficiency is paramount; recent work has introduced dedicated accelerators like Navion, which enable real-time visual-inertial odometry on nano-drones with minimal power draw ref [60]. Moreover, vision-based methods have evolved beyond single-vehicle SLAM to swarm-wide visual-inertial odometry, allowing distributed state estimation without centralized processing ref [84]. These systems are increasingly integrated with reactive obstacle avoidance and collision prediction algorithms, ensuring safe navigation in dynamic, unstructured environments.

The convergence of low-cost sensors, efficient algorithms, and embedded computing has made fully autonomous swarm navigation feasible without reliance on external localization. However, challenges remain in maintaining consistency across heterogeneous platforms, managing perception latency at high speeds, and ensuring robustness to environmental variability. Future directions include hybrid sensing modalities—such as integrating ultra-wideband or acoustic cues with vision—to enhance reliability, and the development of neuromorphic hardware to further reduce power consumption while preserving real-time performance.

subsections.section_title: The Challenge of Local Sensing and Control
subsections.content:
Minimalist navigation for swarm exploration emphasizes lightweight, computationally efficient strategies that enable large teams of micro air vehicles (MAVs) to autonomously map and navigate unknown environments without relying on external infrastructure or heavy onboard processing. The swarm gradient bug algorithm (SGBA) exemplifies this paradigm, leveraging visual odometry and wall-following behaviors to navigate obstacles while maintaining collective coverage through directional dispersion from a home beacon, enabling efficient exploration and homing ref [87]. This approach avoids the resource intensity of simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), instead prioritizing reactive, decentralized decision-making that scales with swarm size. Complementary methods have explored bioinspired obstacle avoidance and gradient-based search heuristics to achieve similar goals under severe computational constraints ref [30]. Recent work has further demonstrated that even with limited sensing—such as single-camera visual flow and ultrasonic proximity detection—swarms can achieve robust exploration by distributing spatial search tasks through simple communication protocols ref [19]. These minimalist systems are particularly suited for indoor, GPS-denied environments where energy efficiency and hardware simplicity are paramount. The integration of low-cost time-of-flight sensors and optical flow units enables real-time navigation without high-end processors, making such systems deployable on commodity platforms like the Crazyflie 2.0 ref [35].

Beyond SGBA, other minimalist frameworks have emerged that exploit emergent collective behavior, such as pheromone-like signaling or local density sensing, to guide exploration without global mapping ref [57]. These strategies reduce communication overhead and increase resilience to individual failures. The use of reactive velocity obstacles and hybrid reciprocal collision avoidance further enhances safety in dense, dynamic swarms during exploration ref [66]. Together, these approaches form a growing toolkit for scalable, low-power swarm exploration, paving the way for applications in disaster response, infrastructure inspection, and planetary exploration where autonomy and robustness outweigh the need for high-fidelity mapping.

subsections.section_title: The Challenge of Local Sensing and Control
subsections.content:
Relative localization in GPS-denied environments is a critical enabler for autonomous micro air vehicle (MAV) swarms, particularly in indoor, urban canyon, or underground scenarios where global navigation satellite systems are unavailable. Recent approaches leverage onboard sensing and inter-agent communication to estimate relative positions without external infrastructure. Ultra-wideband (UWB) ranging has emerged as a robust solution, enabling cooperative relative localization through pairwise distance measurements and exchanged self-displacement data, as demonstrated in a two-stage extended Kalman filter framework that initializes and refines relative poses among UAVs ref [38]. Alternatively, vision-based methods have shown promise by fusing monocular imagery with inertial measurements to achieve onboard visual-inertial odometry (VIO), allowing swarms to maintain relative formation without GPS or external tracking systems, as validated in a 12-quadrotor swarm operating in diverse indoor and outdoor environments ref [12].

Beyond UWB and VIO, hybrid systems integrating low-cost sensors such as ultrasound, optical flow, and acoustic arrays offer scalable alternatives for dense formations. For instance, audio-based localization has been explored to estimate relative bearings among MAVs using distributed microphone arrays ref [63], while lightweight visual-inertial accelerators like Navion enable real-time state estimation on nano-drones with minimal power consumption ref [61]. These methods collectively address the trade-offs between accuracy, computational load, and energy efficiency, which are paramount for resource-constrained MAVs. Moreover, decentralized estimation frameworks, such as distributed smoothing and mapping (DF-SAM 2.0), facilitate consistent relative localization across large swarms without centralized coordination ref [36]. The convergence of these sensing modalities and distributed algorithms is paving the way for robust, scalable, and truly autonomous swarm operations in GPS-denied domains.

subsections.section_title: The Challenge of Local Sensing and Control
subsections.subsection_title: Communication and Control Constraints in Dense Formations
subsections.content: Dense formations of micro air vehicles (MAVs) impose stringent constraints on communication and control due to limited bandwidth, high interference, and tight spatial proximity. In such configurations, traditional broadcast-based communication protocols often suffer from packet collisions and latency spikes, undermining real-time coordination. The Crazyswarm system addresses this by employing compressed one-way data flow over shared radio channels, enabling reliable control of up to 49 nano-quadcopters with sub-centimeter localization accuracy, while offloading computation to onboard processors to minimize latency ref [89]. However, communication range remains a critical bottleneck when paired with physical dynamics: fixed-wing MAVs, constrained by minimum forward velocity and low turning rates, require sufficient communication range to sustain interaction durations long enough for flocking behaviors to emerge, as demonstrated in Reynolds-inspired experiments where insufficient range led to fragmented cohesion ref [88]. This interplay between communication range, vehicle agility, and formation density necessitates co-design of communication protocols and control laws. Decentralized approaches that leverage local sensing—such as on-board relative bearing estimation via sound or optical flow—can reduce reliance on radio communication, but introduce trade-offs in accuracy and scalability. Moreover, dense formations amplify the risk of control instability due to coupled dynamics, requiring robust collision avoidance mechanisms that operate under communication constraints without centralized coordination.

subsections.section_title: The Challenge of Local Sensing and Control
subsections.subsection_title: Swarm Coordination for Physical Construction Tasks
subsections.content:
Swarm coordination for physical construction tasks represents a paradigm shift in automated building, where teams of micro air vehicles (MAVs) collaboratively assemble structures without fixed infrastructure. The Flight Assembled Architecture installation demonstrated the feasibility of aerial construction by deploying four quadrotors to assemble a 6-meter tower from 1,500 foam modules in a public setting, highlighting challenges in safety, robustness, and real-time coordination under human interaction ref [90]. Complementing this, Lindsey et al. introduced a systematic approach using quadrotor teams to assemble 2.5-D truss-like structures from magnetized nodes and members, embedding assembly constraints directly into control algorithms to ensure structural feasibility and task completion ref [91]. These systems require precise spatiotemporal coordination, gripper design for passive attachment, and decentralized planning to avoid collisions during payload transport and placement. Recent work has extended these concepts to modular, self-assembling aerial units capable of in-flight reconfiguration, enabling dynamic structural adaptation ref [62]. Coordination must also account for load balancing, task allocation under uncertainty, and fault tolerance—critical for large-scale deployment. While simulations and small-scale experiments have validated core algorithms, scaling to full-size construction demands advances in energy efficiency, real-time perception, and human-swarm interaction protocols.

Emerging frameworks integrate bioinspired swarm behaviors with task-specific constraints, enabling emergent assembly patterns without centralized control. The use of magnetized components simplifies alignment and reduces the need for high-precision actuation, while vision-based feedback ensures accurate placement in GPS-denied environments. However, the lack of standardized structural vocabularies and the difficulty of scaling beyond 2.5-D geometries remain open challenges. Future directions include hybrid systems combining aerial and ground-based agents, and the integration of real-time structural integrity monitoring during assembly.
